Coach Joe Tartamella has the Red Storm in the N.C.A.A. tournament for the fourth straight year.
A sometimes wrenching adjustment to a new coach in Joe Tartamella, the season-ending injury to the senior guardEugeneia McPhersonin the sixth game and a three-game slide that dropped St. John’s to 9-9 were all part of a testing journey to an18-12 recordand anat-large berth.
“If you look at our group, their resiliency got us to where we are now, because they could have unraveled,” Tartamella said of his team, seeded 10th in the Bridgeport region.
Tartamella, 33, had been a member of Kim Barnes Arico’s staff for the last nine years, helping her to transform a downtrodden program into one that reached the Round of 16 for the first time last year. When Barnes Arico ended her 10-year stay at St. John’s to coach at Michigan, Tartamella emerged as the logical choice to succeed her and was hired last April 27.
Although he had been the associate head coach for four years, Tartamella noted that the transition involved far more than changing his title.
“As everyone will tell you, it’s different sitting in the other seat,” he said. “Until you experience it, you really can just speculate on what it’s like. As an assistant, we give suggestions, and the head coach can either take the suggestions or not take them. As head coach, you’ve got to make the decisions.”
Tartamella also realized that his interaction with his players needed to change. After befriending players he had recruited and being so approachable to them that he was casually referred to as Joey T, he knew he needed to become more of an authority figure while still letting them know he cared for them beyond the court.
“I tried not to change who I am, and I think they understood and respected that,” Tartamella said. “At the same time, it was different because I was not an assistant anymore, not one to be leaning on every day. I’ve got to be the leader for the group. I’ve got to be hard on them at times when they are not used to my being hard.”
As players were growing accustomed to Coach T, they had a major setback when McPherson tore the anterior cruciate ligament in her right knee while driving the lane in a Nov. 25 game at Hartford. Teammates were stunned as McPherson writhed in pain.
“I was like, No, this can’t be happening,” said Briana Brown, a junior who helped fill the void. “It was one of those things where you know exactly what happened, but it still feels surreal.”
Of McPherson’s steadying influence, Brown said: “I can’t explain how hard it was to lose her. She was kind of a glue player. She still is off the court.”
St. John’s became inconsistent, a team with obvious talent but one unable to stitch together prolonged stretches of good basketball. Finally, after a 57-54 defeat at Louisville on Jan. 27 gave the Red Storm their third straight loss and dropped them to .500, the nice-guy coach had enough. Tartamella provided “aggressive counseling” during a 20-minute meeting at which his raised voice was the only one heard.
“He was just wanting to make sure we were all on the same page, that we all wanted to reach the same goal,” said Nadirah McKenith, a senior guard who holds the team record for career assists with 595. “He was pretty angry. I hadn’t seen him like that.”
It was perhaps pivotal for a fresh-faced coach who started as a graduate assistant at St. John’s in 2002.
“It was a turning point,” he said of his outburst’s effect on his players. “It could have been a breaking point, too. I had a feeling it was getting there.”
St. John’s responded by winning seven of its next eight games and playing well in its lone defeat, 71-65, to Connecticut at home on Feb. 2. Despite a 62-55 loss to Louisville in the quarterfinals of the Big East tournament, the Red Storm appear to have found their stride at the ideal time as they brace for Dayton (27-2), the Atlantic 10 regular-season champion. Aliyyah Handford, a 5-foot-9 freshman guard who is a blur on the fast break, emerged as a three-time Big East rookie of the week. Shenneika Smith, the Red Storm’s fourth-leading career scorer with 1,709 points, averages a team-leading 16.7 points a game. She brings the been-there, done-that maturity of a senior.
Asked her hopes for the N.C.A.A. tournament, she replied: “Win on Sunday. That’s our expectation. You look toward something else, and you forget what’s in front of you.”
